Brand vs Performance Marketing: Different Time Horizons

Growth

In short: Brand and performance marketing are not rivals; they work on different clocks. Performance buys measurable outcomes now, while brand makes future outcomes more likely and cheaper. Most small companies should fund performance first, then shift a growing share toward brand, measuring each on its own timescale.

Key points

  • Performance marketing is judged in days or weeks on cost per outcome; brand marketing is judged over months or years.
  • Rising cost per outcome over time is the bill for brand work that was not done.
  • Brand lowers the cost of performance, performance funds brand, and performance generates the evidence brand needs.
  • A company past its first channel might put roughly three quarters of spend on performance and a quarter on brand.
  • Founders with an existing audience, or companies in restricted categories, can compress the usual performance-first sequence.

Marketing teams have argued about brand versus performance for as long as both words have existed. The argument is real, but it is mostly about time.

The two, defined

Performance marketing is spending aimed at a measurable outcome in a short window: a click, a lead, an account, a purchase, attributed to the spend that produced it. It is judged in days or weeks, on cost per outcome. Its tools are the auction platforms, affiliate, creator programs on cost-per-outcome terms, programmatic optimized to conversions.

Brand marketing is spending aimed at changing what people know, believe, or feel about the company, so that future outcomes become more likely and cheaper. It is judged over months or years, on recall, consideration, preference, and, eventually, on the falling cost of performance marketing. Its tools are content, earned media, events, sponsorship, design, consistent presence, and advertising that explains rather than asks.

Why they look like rivals

They compete for the same budget and report on different clocks. In any given quarter, performance marketing can show what it produced and brand marketing cannot. The finance team, reasonably, funds what it can see.

Over several quarters, the reverse problem appears. Performance marketing on its own gets more expensive: the easiest customers are found first, the auctions get more crowded, and the company is buying every customer from scratch because nobody has heard of it. The rising cost per outcome is the bill for the brand work that was not done.

How they interact

Brand lowers the cost of performance. People who recognize a company click more, convert more, and cost less to acquire. Every performance marketer has seen the same ad perform differently for a known brand and an unknown one.

Performance funds brand. Without a working acquisition engine, there is no revenue to invest in the slow work.

And performance generates the evidence brand needs. The language customers respond to, the objections that stop them, the segments that convert: these come from the performance side and should inform what the brand side says.

The honest constraints for a small company

A company with limited cash cannot fund work with an eighteen-month payback, however sound. The sequence for most small companies is performance first, to find a channel that produces customers at a survivable cost, then a growing share of budget toward owned and earned brand work as revenue allows.

Two exceptions. A company with an existing distribution asset, a founder with a following, a list, a community, can do brand work cheaply from day one, because the audience already exists. And a company in a category the ad platforms restrict is pushed toward earned and owned channels early, because the performance auctions are partly closed to it. In both cases, the usual sequence compresses.

A working division

For a company past its first channel: roughly three quarters of spend on performance, measured on cost per outcome against customer value; roughly a quarter on brand, measured on branded search, direct traffic, recall where it can be surveyed, and, above all, the trend in performance cost per outcome over time. Adjust the split as the trend moves.

The point is not the ratio. It is that both sides are funded, both are measured on their own clock, and the company understands that the second one is what makes the first one affordable.

lowob takeaway: Performance marketing buys outcomes now; brand marketing makes future outcomes cheaper. Fund performance first to survive, then brand to stop paying full price for every customer, and measure each on its own clock.

Common questions

What is the difference between brand marketing and performance marketing?

Performance marketing aims at a measurable outcome in a short window, such as a click, lead or purchase, judged on cost per outcome. Brand marketing aims at changing what people know, believe or feel about a company, judged over months or years on recall, consideration and the falling cost of performance marketing.

How should a small company split its budget between brand and performance?

Most small companies should start with performance to find a channel that produces customers at a survivable cost. Once past the first channel, a working division is roughly three quarters on performance and a quarter on brand, adjusted as the trend in cost per outcome moves.

How do you measure brand marketing?

Measure it on branded search, direct traffic, recall where it can be surveyed, and above all the trend in performance cost per outcome over time.

Why does performance marketing get more expensive over time?

The easiest customers are found first, auctions get more crowded, and the company keeps buying every customer from scratch because nobody has heard of it.
